newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian army hits rebels, trashes talk of peace.
newsitem.headline: Colombian army hits rebels, trashes talk of peace.

text.p: A counterinsurgency sweep through northwest Colombia that has claimed at least 17 lives entered its third day on Tuesday, but rebel landmines were hampering army troop movements, authorities said.

Gen. Rito Alejo del Rio, commander of the 17th Army Brigade, said 15 Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas and two soldiers had been killed in the fighting since Sunday in the notoriously violent region of Uraba, near Colombia's border with Panama.

Del Rio, who spoke in an interview with the Radionet news network, said two counterinsurgency battalions continued in pursuit of a 200-strong FARC column early on Tuesday. But he said their advance was slowed by landmines planted by the rebels before retreating toward a stronghold in the Serrania Abibe mountains, outside the Caribbean port of Turbo.

One of the four soldiers injured in the fighting so far was wounded by a FARC landmine, Del Rio said, adding that the guerrilla group had lied in claiming that it no longer uses the so-called "leg-breaking" devices.
"They are planting mines throughout the countryside in Uraba," Del Rio said.

The fighting in Uraba erupted while the FARC was staging a high-profile ceremony on Sunday in southern Caqueta province, where it released 70 captive troops. Sixty of the soldiers had been held since Aug. 30 of last year, when the FARC overran a remote military base and dealt the Colombian army one of its most humiliating defeats in more than 30 years of war.
The troops were released after the government bowed to demands for a provisional demilitarization of a vast jungle area of Caqueta long known for the production of cocaine.
While the temporary retreat is known to have infuriated military commanders, President Ernesto Samper's government said it hopes the troop release will jump-starting peace talks with the FARC.

But armed forces commander Gen. Harold Bedoya, who accuses the rebels of earning millions of dollars a year from drug trafficking and the protection of rural coca farms and cocaine laboratories, poured cold water on talk of peace in scathing remarks to reporters late on Monday.
Bedoya, who human rights activists accuse of tacitly supporting right-wing paramilitary groups that kill with impunity, said of the FARC's claim to legitimacy as a political force:
"When you see drug traffickers calling themselves politicians, that's part of a circus."
